name: AI for School and Educational Leaders 6: Productivity and Workflow Automation
objectives: Given a typical week, list your repeatable admin tasks with minutes spent and choose the top three AI candidates, listing at least ten tasks and keeping judgment about specific students with you

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting time back for communication and meetings

lessons.title: Lesson 1: A time audit: where does the week go?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find your three biggest repeatable time drains.
This lesson builds toward: Given a typical week, you will list your repeatable admin tasks with minutes spent and choose the top three AI candidates, listing at least ten tasks and keeping judgment about specific students with you.
Before automating, measure. For one week, jot down repeatable admin tasks and roughly how long each takes: emails, newsletters, meeting prep, notes, forms, reports, schedules, duty rosters.
Circle tasks that are repeated often, follow a similar pattern each time, and do not need private student information to draft. These are your best AI candidates. Tasks that require judgment about a specific student or staff member stay with you.
Pick your top three by time spent. Those are the workflows you will build in this course, and your before-numbers for measuring time saved.
Step by step:
- For a week, list repeatable admin tasks and minutes spent.
- Circle frequent, patterned tasks that need no private student data.
- Keep judgment-about-people tasks with you.
- Pick the top three by time.
- Save the minutes as your before-numbers.
Words to know:
- Time audit: tracking how you spend your time so you can improve it.
- Workflow: the steps you follow to get a recurring task done.
Try it now: List at least ten repeatable admin tasks from your week with rough minutes for each. Circle your top three AI candidates.
You can now find the repeatable tasks where AI can save you the most time.

options: A review of your school's budget
Tracking how much time you spend on each task
A check of staff attendance
A test of how fast AI works
check.why: A time audit shows where the week goes, so you can pick what to improve.

check.q: One of your time drains is deciding a specific student's discipline. Should it be an AI candidate?
options: Yes, AI is faster
Yes, if no one finds out
No; judgment about a specific student stays with you
Only on busy weeks
check.why: Tasks that need judgment about a specific student stay with the person.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Newsletters and family messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn bullet notes into a clear family newsletter with a reusable prompt.
This lesson builds toward: Given bullet notes for the week, you will turn the notes into a family newsletter with a saved, reusable prompt, checking every date, time and place, with translations checked by a qualified speaker.
Keep a running list of bullet notes during the week: events, dates, reminders, celebrations (no student names unless your school's media and directory-information rules allow it). On Friday, paste the bullets with a saved prompt.
A reusable prompt: "Turn these notes into a warm, clear family newsletter for an elementary school. Plain English, short sections with headings, dates in bold, under 300 words. Do not add any event or fact that is not in my notes." Save it so the newsletter looks consistent every week.
Check every date, time and place against the school calendar. For families who read other languages, an AI translation is a draft: have a qualified speaker check it before it goes out, so families get accurate information.
Step by step:
- Keep bullet notes during the week.
- Paste them with your saved newsletter prompt.
- Check every date, time and place.
- Have translations checked by a qualified speaker.
- Send, and save the prompt for next week.
Words to know:
- Reusable prompt: a prompt you save and use every time for the same task.
- Qualified speaker: a person fluent enough in a language to check a translation for accuracy.
Try it now: Write bullet notes for a made-up week and use the saved prompt to turn them into a newsletter. Check it against your notes and time how long it took.
You can now produce a consistent, checked family newsletter from weekly notes.

options: So you can reuse it each week
So the AI remembers your students
So families can see it
So it never needs checking
check.why: A saved prompt makes the weekly newsletter repeatable.

check.q: The AI newsletter lists a bake sale that is not in your notes. What would you do?
options: Keep it; families like bake sales
Change the date
Send it and correct it later
Remove it and add "Do not add anything not in my notes" to the prompt
check.why: AI can invent events, so the prompt forbids it and you check against your notes.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Meetings: agenda to action list
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft an agenda and turn notes into an action list with owners and dates.
This lesson builds toward: For a staff or team meeting, you will draft a timed agenda with AI and turn notes into an action list with owners and dates, sending the action list the same day.
Before: give AI the meeting purpose, length, attendees by role, and topics. Ask for a timed agenda with the desired outcome for each item (decide, discuss, inform). Send it ahead so people come ready.
After: paste your notes (with personal details about students or staff removed) and ask for decisions, actions as a table with owner and due date, and open questions, with "write MISSING if an owner or date is not in the notes; add nothing that is not in the notes".
Check the action list against your memory, fill gaps and send it the same day. If you consider an AI meeting recorder, check your district policy and tell participants first; never record meetings about individual students, such as IEP or discipline meetings, with unapproved tools.
Step by step:
- Draft a timed agenda with outcomes per item.
- Send it ahead.
- After the meeting, paste notes with personal details removed.
- Get decisions, actions (owner, date) and open questions.
- Check, fill gaps and send the same day.
Words to know:
- Agenda: the list of topics and timings for a meeting.
- Action list: tasks agreed in a meeting, each with an owner and a due date.
Try it now: Use AI to draft a timed agenda for your next staff or team meeting. After it, turn your notes into an action list and send it the same day. Time both steps.
You can now run meetings from a clear agenda to a same-day action list with AI's help.

check.q: What does a timed agenda give each item?
options: A time and a desired outcome
A speaker's salary
A vote
A slide deck
check.why: Times and outcomes keep the meeting focused.

check.q: A team wants to record an IEP meeting with a free, unapproved AI recorder. What would you say?
options: Go ahead, it saves notes
Record it but delete it later
No; use only approved tools and follow policy for student meetings
Record only half of it
check.why: IEP meetings involve protected student information and need approved tools and policy.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Forms, automations and measuring the gain

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Surveys and forms: from responses to a summary
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Summarize survey results with AI without exposing personal information.
This lesson builds toward: Given survey responses with no names, you will summarize the results with AI and check the counts against the responses, with names, emails and identifying comments removed first.
Google Forms and Microsoft Forms collect responses into a spreadsheet. AI can then help you see themes in open comments and write a short summary for staff or families.
Protect people first. Design surveys that do not collect names unless you truly need them. Before pasting responses into an AI tool, delete names, emails and any comment that identifies a student or staff member. Use only approved tools for anything containing student information.
Prompt: "Here are anonymous survey comments from families about pickup times. Group them into themes, count how many fit each theme, quote two short typical comments per theme, and list three suggestions. Do not invent comments." Then check the counts yourself against the spreadsheet; AI often miscounts.
Step by step:
- Design surveys without names unless needed.
- Remove names, emails and identifying comments before using AI.
- Use approved tools for anything with student information.
- Ask for themes, counts, typical quotes and suggestions.
- Check the counts yourself.
Words to know:
- Anonymous: without names or details that show who someone is.
- Theme: a common idea that appears in many responses.
Try it now: Create a three-question anonymous survey in Google Forms or Microsoft Forms. Write ten made-up responses, summarize them with AI, and check the counts against the responses.
You can now turn survey responses into an accurate summary without exposing personal information.

options: It has a short title
It does not collect names or identifying details
Only the principal reads it
It is sent by email
check.why: Anonymous surveys collect no names or identifying details.

check.q: AI says 40 families mentioned parking. What do you do before reporting it?
options: Check the count against the spreadsheet of responses
Report it as is
Round it up to 50
Ask the AI if it is sure
check.why: AI counts can be wrong, so check them against the data.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Simple automations: templates, rules and triggers
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up one simple automation and keep a human check in it.
This lesson builds toward: For one common task, you will set up a simple automation, such as an email template or sorting rule, with a human check, tested on yourself first and approved by your technology team where needed.
Not everything needs AI. Many time savers are simple automations: email templates for common replies, email rules that sort messages into folders, document templates for recurring reports, mail merge for personalized letters, and calendar reminders.
Bigger automations connect steps: when a form is submitted, add a row to a sheet and send a confirmation; every Friday, remind staff to submit notes. Microsoft Power Automate and Google Apps Script can do this; ask your technology team what is allowed in your district before building anything that touches school data.
Keep a human check wherever an automation sends something to families or makes a change that matters. A small mistake repeated automatically to 500 families is a big mistake.
Step by step:
- Start simple: templates, rules, reminders.
- Pick one repeated task to automate.
- Check with your technology team before connecting school data.
- Add a human check before anything goes to families.
- Test with yourself as the only recipient first.
Words to know:
- Automation: a set-up that does a task automatically when something happens.
- Trigger: the event that starts an automation, like a form being submitted.
- Mail merge: making many personalized letters or emails from one template and a list.
Try it now: Set up one simple automation: an email template for a common reply, or a rule that sorts a type of message. Test it on yourself and write where the human check is.
You can now set up simple automations safely, with a human check where it matters.

check.q: What is a trigger in an automation?
options: The person who approves it
The last step of the workflow
The event that starts the automation
A type of email
check.why: A trigger, such as a new message arriving, starts the automation.

check.q: You built a rule that replies to families automatically. What do you do first?
options: Turn it on for all families at once
Turn it off and forget it
Ask families to test it
Test it with yourself as the only recipient
check.why: Testing on yourself catches mistakes before they reach many people.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring time saved and keeping it going
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Measure before-and-after time and make your workflows last.
This lesson builds toward: After running your workflows for a week, you will measure before-and-after minutes and write each workflow on one page, counting checking and fixing time, and saving the pages in a shared folder.
You saved time only if the numbers say so. For each workflow, compare minutes before (from your time audit) and after, including checking time. If a workflow takes as long because of fixing, change the prompt or drop the workflow.
Write each workflow on one page: the purpose, the saved prompt or template, the steps, the human check, and who does it. Then someone else can run it when you are out, and new staff can learn it.
Share wins with staff and invite their workflows. A shared folder of school prompts and templates multiplies the time saved across the building. Review it each term so prompts stay accurate as calendars, tools and policies change.
Step by step:
- Compare minutes before and after, including checking.
- Fix or drop workflows that do not save time.
- Write each workflow on one page.
- Share in a school prompt and template folder.
- Review every term.
Words to know:
- Before-and-after: comparing a measure before and after a change.
- Documentation: written steps so others can repeat a process.
Try it now: Final task: run your three workflows for one week (newsletter, meeting agenda to actions, survey to summary). Record before and after minutes for each, write each on one page with its human check, and put them in a shared folder.
You can now build, measure and share AI-assisted admin workflows that give time back to students.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Newsletter workflow The newsletter was not checked against the notes, or a translation went unchecked. Bullet notes became a finished, checked draft, with any translation checked by a qualified speaker. Uses a saved prompt that forbids adding anything not in the notes. Meeting workflow No action list, or tasks without owners or dates. An AI-drafted agenda and an action list with owners and dates, sent the same day. Missing owners are marked and followed up. Survey workflow The data included names, or counts were not checked. Survey results summarized with AI using only data with no names. Counts were checked against the spreadsheet and typical comments quoted for each theme. Time measured No before or after minutes recorded. Before and after minutes recorded for each workflow. After minutes include checking and fixing time. Human checks A workflow sends something to families with no human check. Each workflow names the human check kept in it. Each workflow is written on one page in a shared folder so others can run it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Only the time AI took to answer
The time spent checking and fixing too
Only the best day of the week
The time others spent
check.why: Checking and fixing time is part of the real cost of a workflow.

check.q: A workflow still takes as long as before because you fix many AI errors. What would you do?
options: Change the prompt or drop the workflow
Keep it, since AI is new
Stop checking the output
Add a second AI tool
check.why: A workflow that saves no time should be improved or dropped.
